title: UK labour market overview — earnings, unemployment and vacancies (ONS, 07:00 London / 02:00 ET), the MPC's last wage read before the 09-17 vote
source: EST: ons.gov.uk/releases/uklabourmarketseptember2026, fetched direct 2026-09-09 (HTTP 200) — the ONS release-calendar entry reads verbatim 'UK Labour Market: September 2026', '15 September 2026 at 7:00am', 'Estimates of employment, unemployment, inactivity, average weekly earnings, vacancies and other labour market related statistics for the UK', marked not yet published. Corroborated from a second ONS primary: the August 2026 bulletin (ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/uklabourmarket/august2026, fetched direct 2026-09-09) states 'Released: 18 August 2026' and 'Next release: 15 September 2026'. Primary-sourced from the publisher's own schedule; filed estimate on this lane's no-self-confirm limit and because the confirmed-prefix taxonomy in market-events-data.ts carries BLS:/BEA:/CENSUS:/ISM: and has no slot for the UK Office for National Statistics. Checked 2026-09-09
notes: CANONICAL FILE WRITTEN BY THE never-assessed INITIAL RESEARCH 2026-09-09, superseding proposals/uk-labour-market-2026-09-15.from-boe-decision-2026-09-17.json (read in full first per docs/process/EVENT-RESEARCH.md). That proposal's placement finding stands and is carried: this is the wage number the MPC's second-round-effects argument is actually about, published 07:00 London on 09-15 — inside the committee's information set for a meeting that ends 09-16 and announces 09-17. WHAT THE INITIAL RESEARCH ADDED: the headline wage figure is a COMPOSITION ARTIFACT and the wires print the wrong cell. In the August release (Apr-Jun 2026) whole-economy regular pay was 3.5% y/y, but that is public sector 6.1% averaged against PRIVATE SECTOR 2.8% — 'the last time private sector regular earnings growth was lower than 2.8% was August to October 2020' (press-cited Reuters read of the ONS series). The MPC's second-round-effects question is a private-sector question, so 2.8% is the cell that settles the 09-17 vote split, not 3.5%. The tape already reads it this way: on 2026-08-18 whole-economy regular pay BEAT the 3.4% Reuters consensus at 3.5% and sterling still FELL 0.1% to $1.352. Second finding, from an ONS primary: the release's own headline unemployment rate is its least reliable cell — LFS outputs are 'official statistics in development', ONS told OSR on 2026-08-11 verbatim 'We will not be seeking reaccreditation for LFS and APS-derived outputs', TLFS transition is no earlier than November 2027 after a July 2027 decision point, and the August bulletin says plainly 'Our view remains that RTI currently provides the most reliable measure of employees.' Level data as of the August bulletin (ONS, fetched 2026-09-09): unemployment 4.9%, employment 75.1%, inactivity 20.9% (Apr-Jun); regular pay +3.5% / total +4.1% / private +2.8% / public +6.1% (Apr-Jun); real regular pay +0.5% CPIH; vacancies 707,000, -6,000 (0.8%) on the quarter (May-Jul), 'outside of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic period, the last time there were 707,000 or fewer vacancies was in September to November 2014'; payrolled employees 30.3m, -13,000 (0.0%) on the month and -94,000 (0.3%) on the year (July early estimate); claimant count 1.665m (July). Tiered LOW and the tier is argued, not assumed: UK-only, symbols: [], no house playbook is rates- or sterling-keyed, and the measured reaction to the last print was ~0.1% in cable — raising it to medium would imply an actionability this book does not have. Estimate widens caution only; it licenses no date-keyed action.
